title: The story inside the story (Mark 5:21–43)
hookLine: Mark sandwiches the bleeding woman inside Jairus's daughter; both are daughters

cards: A father falls at a teacher's feet, begging him to come: his little girl is dying. They set off through a pressing crowd, and every minute counts. And then the teacher stops.
Mark does something you saw on day two hundred: he starts one story, stops it halfway, tells a whole second story in the middle, and only then finishes the first. Scholars call it a Markan sandwich.
And the two stories turn out to be mirrors of each other.

teach.b: First, the outside story. Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, an important man, falls at Jesus's feet. My little daughter is dying, he says; come and lay your hands on her.
Jesus goes, and the crowd presses in around him. Second, the inside story.
In that crowd is a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years. She's spent everything on doctors and only got worse, and under the law the bleeding also kept her ritually unclean.
She thinks: if I can just touch his clothes. She does, and she feels it: she's healed. And Jesus stops.
"Who hath touched my garments?" The disciples point out the obvious: the whole crowd is pressing on you. Meanwhile Jairus stands there, his daughter dying, and Jesus waits.
The woman comes forward, trembling, and tells him the whole truth. He says: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace." Third, the bad news.
While he's still speaking, messengers arrive: your daughter is dead; why trouble the master any further?
Jesus turns to Jairus: "Fear not, only believe." At the house, he takes the girl by the hand and says: talitha cumi. Mark keeps the words as Jesus said them, then translates: damsel, arise.
She gets up and walks, and Jesus tells them to give her something to eat. Fourth, the mirrors.
The woman has been sick twelve years; the girl is twelve years old.

teach.h: DAUGHTER, THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.
teach.b: Both are called daughter. Both are unclean by the law, one bleeding, one dead. She touches him; he takes the girl by the hand.
And the interruption that looked like it cost the girl her life turns out to be part of the same healing.

how: Catholics hear the raising of Jairus's daughter and the healing of the woman at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time (Year B), and the Church prays for the sick through the sacrament of anointing.

o: a blessing: go in peace, child
a call to the little girl: arise
a prayer: let her faith heal her

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: fell at his feet for his daughter

s: the woman and the girl are linked by the number twelve
twelve years of bleeding; a girl twelve years old.
Jesus kept walking after the woman was healed
he stopped and asked, who touched my garments? and waited for her.
after raising the girl, Jesus told them to give her something to eat
a small, very human detail Mark keeps.

games.q: you're hurrying to a dying girl, and you feel someone in the crowd touch your clothes. every minute counts. what does Jesus do?
o: stop and ask who touched him, and wait for her.
send a disciple to find her later.
games.why: he stops: "Who hath touched my garments?" he waits, hears her whole story, and calls her daughter.

practice: Think back over the last day or two: who stopped you on your way somewhere? A child with a question, a coworker at your desk, a text from someone who needed to talk; pick one, and ask what they actually needed.
If you pray, hold that person before God and ask to see the next interruption differently; if you don't, picture yourself stopping for them, the way Jesus stopped.

wordCard.voice: Talitha cumi. Aramaic for little girl, arise: Jesus's words to Jairus's daughter. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters: little girl, arise; Mark keeps Jesus's own words.

carryVoice: Your line: interruptions are the ministry. Jesus stopped, and the girl still rose. That's two hundred five.

sources.q: Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace
